items.title: A coin doesn't 'owe' you a head after 10 tails — but a casino does
items.claim: 10 tails in a row. Probability of the next flip being heads is still 1/2. The coin has no memory. Casinos exploit the gambler's fallacy — players betting against 'streaks' actually have no edge.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the law of large numbers help short-term?

options.text: The law of large numbers only applies to dice

LLN guarantees long-run frequency convergence to expected probability, but does NOT mean short-term deviations must be 'corrected' by reverse outcomes. Each flip is independent: past results carry no information
Tails must come back to balance heads

items.reveal_title: Gambler's fallacy and the law of large numbers (correctly stated)
items.reveal:
Gambler's fallacy: the false belief that, in a sequence of independent random events, recent 'streaks' make the opposite outcome more likely.

Monte Carlo Casino, 1913: black came up 26 times in a row at a roulette table. Players reportedly lost millions betting on red, believing the streak 'must' end. Each spin was independent; the probability of red on the 27th spin was the same as on the first (~18/37 for a European wheel, less than 1/2 because of the green zero).

LLN says: as n increases, the SAMPLE PROPORTION approaches the TRUE PROBABILITY. After 10 tails in a row out of 10 flips, the proportion is 100% tails. After a million more fair flips (with roughly 500,000 each side), the cumulative proportion approaches 50%. But this happens by SWAMPING the early streak, not by REVERSING it. The next flip after 10 tails is still 50/50.

Inverse mistake (hot-hand fallacy): assuming streaks WILL continue (sports). Actually mixed evidence — some sports skills appear to genuinely streak (basketball shooting under some studies), others don't. Distinguishing real streaks from spurious ones requires careful statistics.

Gambler's fallacy explains casino profits even when individual games are 'fair-ish'. House edges (~5% in roulette) compound over many bets; players betting against streaks don't gain anything.

The broader cognitive pattern: humans expect randomness to be uniform. Real randomness has clusters and streaks. Mistaking real randomness for 'patterns' is one of the most consistently studied errors in cognitive psychology.
items.why: Past results feel like they should influence future probabilities. They don't, for independent events. Misunderstanding this drives gambling losses, conspiracy theories, and bad predictions across domains.

items.title: Computers compute sine by adding up polynomials
items.claim: Your calculator can't 'compute sine'. It computes a polynomial that approximates sine very accurately. Specifically, sin(x) = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 - x^7/5040 + ... The Taylor series gives any function as a sum of polynomial terms.

options.text: Polynomials and sine are always equal
Any analytic function f(x) can be expressed as a power series sum of f^(n)(a) * (x-a)^n / n!; truncating to a few terms gives a polynomial approximation with rigorously bounded error near x = a
Only sine has a Taylor series

items.reveal:
Taylor series: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)(x-a)^2/2! + f'''(a)(x-a)^3/3! + ...

For analytic functions (most functions arising in physics and engineering), the series converges to f(x) within a radius of convergence around a.

Key examples around a = 0 (Maclaurin):
sin(x) = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - x^7/7! + ... (converges for all real x)
cos(x) = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - x^6/6! + ... (converges for all real x)
e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... (converges for all real x)
ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ... (converges for |x| < 1)
1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + ... (converges for |x| < 1, geometric)

For small x, truncating after a few terms gives good approximation. For sin(x), keeping x - x^3/6 gives error of about x^5/120; for x = 0.1, error ~ 10^(-8).

Calculators use TWO TRICKS:
1. Argument reduction: reduce sin(x) for large x to sin(x') where x' is in a small range, using periodicity and symmetries.
2. Polynomial approximation: minimax polynomials (Chebyshev-optimal) often beat Taylor for fixed precision.

Applications:
- Computer hardware (FPUs): implement transcendental functions via polynomial approximation.
- Numerical analysis: many algorithms (Newton-Raphson, Runge-Kutta) involve Taylor expansion.
- Physics: small-angle approximations (sin x ≈ x, cos x ≈ 1) are first-order Taylor.
- Perturbation theory in quantum mechanics: expansion of solutions around exactly-solvable cases.

Divergent Taylor series: some functions have Taylor series that converge only at a single point (formal series that don't represent the function). These appear in asymptotic analysis (Stirling's approximation, certain physics calculations).
items.why: Functions like sine seem 'analytical' or special. Computationally, they're polynomial approximations. The Taylor expansion is the practical universal interface between abstract functions and computers.

items.title: A sphere can be cut into five pieces that reassemble into TWO spheres
items.claim: The Banach-Tarski paradox (1924): a solid ball in 3D can be divided into a finite number of pieces (just five) which, by rigid rotation, reassemble into two solid balls each the same size as the original.
items.prompt: Doesn't this violate conservation of volume?

options.text: The pieces are not 'volumes' in any classical sense — they are extremely complicated point sets that cannot be assigned any consistent volume (they are 'non-measurable'); volume is conserved among measurable sets, and these aren't
Volume is doubled by the rotations

items.reveal_title: Non-measurable sets and the Axiom of Choice
items.reveal:
Banach and Tarski showed the result follows from the Axiom of Choice (AC) — the assertion that for any collection of non-empty sets, you can pick one element from each.

AC lets you construct sets that are too complicated to have a well-defined volume. These 'non-measurable' sets exist only as mathematical objects; you can't physically separate a ball into them.

Without AC, the paradox does not hold. Banach-Tarski has been used by some mathematicians as an argument against AC. Most accept AC anyway because giving it up loses too many other useful results.

This is not a chemistry or physics result — gold atoms have volume, and you cannot duplicate a gold ball this way. It's about the foundational assumptions of mathematics.
items.why: Common sense assumes any reasonable subset of space has a size. Set theory shows you can construct subsets with no size — and they can be reassembled in unsettling ways.
